title: Environments
summary: Keep different settings — like API URLs — for development and production.
heading: Environments

blocks.text: Your app needs different settings depending on where it runs. In development the API is http://localhost:3000; in production it's your real server. Hard-coding URLs means editing code before every deploy. Environment files hold these settings separately, and Angular swaps them in automatically at build time.
The CLI scaffolds the environment files and wires them into the build for you.
It creates two files. The base one is used for production; the .development one overrides it during development.

blocks.label: src/environments/environment.ts
src/environments/environment.development.ts

blocks.text: ng generate environments adds a file replacement to angular.json. During a development build, Angular replaces environment.ts with environment.development.ts — so your imports stay the same, but the values change.
ng serve uses the development configuration (so you get the dev values); ng build defaults to production (the base file).
Always import from environment.ts (no suffix). Angular substitutes the right file for the build. A service is the perfect place to use it — instead of a hard-coded URL.

blocks.label: user.service.ts

blocks.text: Environment files are bundled into the browser, so never put secrets (API keys, passwords) in them — anyone can read the shipped code. Keep secrets on the server.

items: Environments hold per-build settings like the API URL.
angular.json file replacement swaps them at build time.
Import from environment.ts everywhere — Angular picks the right one.
Never store secrets — env values ship to the browser.
